hints: Start by thinking about what diploid means in most body cells - two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent. What would the opposite of that look like?
Focus on sets and pairs - how many sets are present, and are the chromosomes found as homologous pairs or as single different chromosomes?
walkthrough:
What chromosome sets mean**
Think of chromosomes as coming in sets. A diploid cell has two sets, written as 2n, with chromosomes in homologous pairs - one of each pair from the mother and one from the father. A haploid cell has only half of that information.

Building the definition of haploid**
Haploid, written as n, means there is only one single set of chromosomes. Because there is only one set, there are no homologous pairs - there is just one of each chromosome, each different in size, shape and genes carried.
Final answer: Having a single set of chromosomes (n chromosomes, half the diploid number) with no homologous pairs, so only one of each type.

hints: Look for the clue words identical versus different. Which process copies cells exactly and which process mixes genes from two parents?
Trace the story for each letter - C grows into a copy of the parent, B makes sperm that fuses, D is the fusion product that makes spores.
Remember where halving must happen - if D is formed by fusion of two haploid gametes, what ploidy is D and what division must it use to get back to haploid spores?
walkthrough:
Spotting sexual reproduction**
Structure C gives plants genetically identical to the parent, so that is asexual. Structure B makes sperm that swims to an egg on another plant and fuses to form D, giving genetically different offspring. That fusion of gametes is sexual reproduction, so B and D are associated with sexual reproduction.

Where mitosis happens**
Mitosis makes genetically identical cells. The haploid thallus grows structures A and B by mitosis, C discs are made by mitosis inside A, sperm in B are made by mitosis, and D also grows by mitosis. Any two from A, B, C, D earns the mark.

Where meiosis must happen**
Egg (n) + sperm (n) fuse to make D, so D is diploid (2n). To make haploid spores that grow into haploid plants again, D must halve the chromosome number. That halving is meiosis, so D is the site of meiosis.
Final answer: associated with sexual reproduction: B and D; produced by mitosis: any two from A, B, C, D; the site of meiosis: D.

hints: Start with the horse body cells - they are diploid. What would happen to chromosome number if two diploid gametes fused?
Think of meiosis as halving and fertilisation as restoring - how does this cycle keep the number constant from parents to offspring?
Consider why variation matters and what goes wrong if the number keeps rising each generation.
walkthrough:
The doubling problem**
Horses are diploid (2n). If gametes were made by mitosis they would also be diploid. Fusion of two diploid gametes would give 4n, then 8n in the next generation, doubling every time.

Halve then restore**
The reduction division of meiosis halves the number from diploid to haploid (2n to n) in sperm and eggs. At fertilisation, n + n restores 2n in the zygote. This maintains the correct diploid chromosome number from parents to offspring in every generation.

Why this matters**
Meiosis also creates genetic variation in gametes and therefore in offspring through independent assortment and crossing over. Keeping the number stable avoids extra sets of chromosomes which would disrupt development and fertility.

Final answer: Meiosis halves chromosome number to produce haploid gametes so that fertilisation restores the diploid number, maintaining it from generation to generation and generating genetic variation; without it chromosome number would double and cause developmental problems.
